subject: tear-drinking moth
title: This Moth Drinks Tears From Sleeping Birds' Eyes With a Barbed Tongue

scenes.text: In Madagascar, birds sleep with a thief perched on their necks.
It's a moth. And it's drinking from the bird's closed eye.
That's hard: a bird has two eyelids, plus a third, see-through one.
So this moth's tongue is armed with sharp barbs. It slides under the lid and holds on.
Scientists described it in 2007, the first known case of a moth feeding on bird tears.
Why tears? Salt. Puddles on the forest floor hide frogs at night. A sleeping bird's neck is safer.

description:
In Madagascar, a moth lands on sleeping birds and drinks their tears through a barbed proboscis slipped under the eyelid.
It was described in Biology Letters in 2007 as the first known case of tear-feeding on birds. Birds have upper and lower lids plus a nictitating membrane, so the moth needs barbs to anchor. The researchers think a sleeping bird is a safer source of salt than a puddle full of frogs.
Would you rather be the moth or the bird?
first_comment: In 2017 another moth was filmed in Brazil drinking a sleeping antbird's tears around 1 a.m. Which insect creeps you out most?
